danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 37
paragraphs: En af lægerne kom ud af teltet i et blodplettet forklæde med en cigar mellem tommelfinger og lillefinger på den ene af sine små blodplettede hænder for ikke at tilsmudse den. Han løftede hovedet og så sig omkring, men over de såredes hoveder. Han havde tydeligvis brug for et lille pusterum. Efter at have drejet hovedet fra højre til venstre i nogen tid sukkede han og så ned.
»I orden, straks,« svarede han til en sygehjælper, der pegede fyrst Andrej ud for ham, og han sagde, at de skulle bære ham ind i teltet.
Der lød mumlen blandt de sårede, der ventede.
»Det ser ud til, at selv i den næste verden er det kun de fine, der får en chance!« bemærkede en.

Fyrst Andrej blev båret ind og lagt på et bord, der lige var blevet ryddet, og som en sygehjælper var ved at vaske af. Fyrst Andrej kunne ikke klart skelne, hvad der var i teltet. De ynkelige stønnen fra alle sider og den pinefulde smerte i hans lår, mave og ryg distraherede ham. Alt, hvad han så omkring sig, smeltede sammen til et generelt indtryk af nøgne, blødende menneskekroppe, der syntes at fylde hele det lave telt, ligesom sådanne kroppe for nogle uger siden, den varme augustdag, havde fyldt den beskidte dam ved vejen til Smolensk. Ja, det var det samme kød, det samme chair à canon, hvis syn allerede dengang havde fyldt ham med rædsel, som en anelse.

Der var tre operationsborde i teltet. To var optaget, og på det tredje lagde de fyrst Andrej. I en kort stund blev han overladt til sig selv og overværede ufrivilligt, hvad der foregik ved de to andre borde. På det nærmeste sad en tatar, sandsynligvis en kosak at dømme efter uniformen, der var kastet ved siden af ham. Fire soldater holdt ham fast, og en brilleforsynet læge skar i hans muskuløse brune ryg.

»Oh, oh, oh!« stønnede tataren, og pludselig løftede han sit mørke, stumpnæsede ansigt med de høje kindben og blottede sine hvide tænder og begyndte at vride og vrikke sin krop og udstøde gennemtrængende, skingrende og langtrukne hyl. På det andet bord, som mange mennesker stimlede sammen om, lå en høj, velnæret mand på ryggen med hovedet kastet bagover. Hans krøllede hår, dets farve og hovedets form syntes mærkelig bekendt for fyrst Andrej. Flere sygehjælpere pressede på hans bryst for at holde ham nede. Det ene store, hvide, fyldige ben rykkede uafladelig med en feberagtig skælven. Manden hulkede og rokkede krampagtigt. To læger — den ene bleg og skælvende — var tavst i gang med noget ved denne mands andet, blodige ben. Da den brilleforsynede læge var færdig med tataren, som de dækkede til med en kappe, kom han hen til fyrst Andrej og tørrede hænderne.
Han kastede et blik på fyrst Andrejs ansigt og vendte sig hurtigt bort.
»Klæd ham af! Hvad venter I på?« råbte han vredt til sygehjælperne.

Hans allerførste, fjerneste barndomsminder vendte tilbage til fyrst Andrejs sind, da sygehjælperen med opsmøgede ærmer hastigt begyndte at knappe hans tøj op og klæde ham af. Lægen bøjede sig over såret, følte på det og sukkede dybt. Derefter gav han tegn til nogen, og den torturerende smerte i hans underliv fik fyrst Andrej til at miste bevidstheden. Da han kom til sig selv, var de splintrede stykker af hans lårbensknogle fjernet, det flænsede kød skåret bort og såret forbundet. Der blev sprinklet vand i hans ansigt. Så snart fyrst Andrej slog øjnene op, bøjede lægen sig over ham, kyssede ham tavst på læberne og skyndte sig væk.

Efter de lidelser, han havde udstået, nød fyrst Andrej en lyksalig følelse, som han ikke havde oplevet i lang tid. Alle de bedste og lykkeligste øjeblikke i hans liv — især hans tidligste barndom, da han blev klædt af og puttet i seng, og da hans amme bøjede sig over ham og sang ham i søvn, og han, med hovedet begravet i puden, følte sig lykkelig blot ved bevidstheden om at leve — vendte tilbage til hans erindring, ikke blot som noget fortidigt, men som noget nærværende.
Lægerne var travlt optaget af den sårede mand, hvis hovedform syntes bekendt for fyrst Andrej: de løftede ham op og forsøgte at berolige ham.
»Vis mig det... Åh, åh... Åh! Åh, åh!« Hans forskræmte jamren kunne høres, dæmpet af lidelse og brudt af hulken.

Da fyrst Andrej hørte disse jammer, ville han græde. Hvad enten det var, fordi han lå for døden uden ære, eller fordi han var ked af at skilles fra livet, eller på grund af de barndomsminder, der ikke kunne vende tilbage, eller fordi han selv led, og andre led, og denne mand nær ham stønnede så ynkeligt — følte han trang til at græde barnlige, venlige og næsten lykkelige tårer.
Den sårede blev vist sit amputerede ben, plettet af størknet blod og med støvlen stadig på.
»Åh! Åh, åh!« hulkede han som en kvinde.
Lægen, der havde stået ved siden af ham og forhindret fyrst Andrej i at se hans ansigt, trådte til side.
»Min Gud! Hvad er dette? Hvorfor er han her?« sagde fyrst Andrej til sig selv.

I den elendige, hulkende, afkræftede mand, hvis ben lige var blevet amputeret, genkendte han Anatol Kuragin. Mænd støttede ham i deres arme og rakte ham et glas vand, men hans skælvende, opsvulmede læber kunne ikke gribe om glassets rand. Anatol hulkede smertefuldt. »Ja, det er ham! Ja, den mand er på en eller anden måde nært og smertefuldt forbundet med mig,« tænkte fyrst Andrej, uden endnu klart at fatte, hvad han så foran sig. »Hvad er forbindelsen mellem den mand og min barndom og mit liv?« spurgte han sig selv uden at finde svar. Og pludselig rejste et nyt, uventet minde sig fra den verden af ren og kærlig barndom. Han huskede Natasja, som han havde set hende for første gang ved ballet i 1810, med hendes slanke hals og arme og med et forskrækket lykkeligt ansigt, rede til henrykkelse, og kærlighed og ømhed for hende, stærkere og mere levende end nogensinde, vågnede i hans sjæl. Han huskede nu den forbindelse, der fandtes mellem ham selv og denne mand, der dunkelt stirrede på ham gennem tårer, der fyldte hans opsvulmede øjne. Han huskede alt, og ekstatisk medlidenhed og kærlighed til denne mand oversvømmede hans lykkelige hjerte.
Fyrst Andrej kunne ikke længere holde sig tilbage og græd ømme, kærlige tårer for sine medmennesker, for sig selv og for sine egne og deres fejl.

»Medlidenhed, kærlighed til vore brødre, til dem der elsker os, og til dem der hader os, kærlighed til vore fjender; ja, den kærlighed, som Gud prædikede på jorden, og som fyrstinde Marja lærte mig, og som jeg ikke forstod — det er det, der fik mig til at være ked af at skilles fra livet, det er det, der var blevet tilbage for mig, hvis jeg havde levet. Men nu er det for sent. Jeg ved det!«

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 37
paragraphs: One of the doctors came out of the tent in a bloodstained apron, holding a cigar between the thumb and little finger of one of his small bloodstained hands so as not to smear it. He raised his head and looked around, above the level of the wounded men. He clearly wanted a brief break. After turning his head from right to left for a while, he sighed and looked down.
"All right, right away," he replied to an attendant who pointed Prince Andrew out to him, and he ordered them to carry him into the tent.
Murmurs arose among the wounded who were waiting.
"So even in the next world only the gentry get a chance!" one of them remarked.

Prince Andrew was carried in and laid on a table that had just been cleared and which an attendant was wiping down. He couldn't make out clearly what was in the tent. The pitiful groans from all sides and the excruciating pain in his thigh, stomach, and back distracted him. Everything he saw around him merged into a single impression of naked, bleeding human bodies that seemed to fill the entire low tent — just as, a few weeks before, on that hot August day, such bodies had filled the dirty pond by the Smolensk road. Yes, it was the same flesh, the same cannon fodder, the sight of which had filled him with horror even then, like a premonition.

There were three operating tables in the tent. Two were occupied, and on the third they laid Prince Andrew. For a while he was left alone and involuntarily witnessed what was happening on the other tables. On the nearest sat a Tatar — probably a Cossack, judging by the uniform tossed beside him. Four soldiers held him down while a bespectacled doctor cut into his muscular brown back.

"Ooh, ooh, ooh!" grunted the Tatar, and suddenly lifting his swarthy, snub-nosed face with its high cheekbones and baring his white teeth, he began to writhe and twist his body, uttering piercing, ringing, drawn-out screams. On the other table, surrounded by many people, a tall, heavyset man lay on his back with his head thrown back. His curly hair, its color, and the shape of his head seemed strangely familiar to Prince Andrew. Several attendants pressed on his chest to hold him still. One large, white, plump leg twitched rapidly with a feverish tremor. The man was sobbing and choking convulsively. Two doctors — one pale and trembling — were silently working on the man's other, blood-soaked leg. When the bespectacled doctor finished with the Tatar, whom they covered with an overcoat, he came over to Prince Andrew, wiping his hands.
He glanced at Prince Andrew's face and quickly looked away.
"Undress him! What are you waiting for?" he said sharply to the attendants.

Prince Andrew's earliest childhood memories came flooding back as the attendant, with sleeves rolled up, began quickly unbuttoning his clothes. The doctor bent over the wound, examined it, and sighed deeply. Then he signaled to someone, and the agonizing pain in his abdomen caused Prince Andrew to lose consciousness. When he came to, the splintered fragments of his thighbone had been extracted, the torn flesh cut away, and the wound bandaged. Water was being sprinkled on his face. The moment Prince Andrew opened his eyes, the doctor bent down, kissed him silently on the lips, and hurried away.

After the suffering he had endured, Prince Andrew experienced a blissful feeling he hadn't known for a long time. All the best and happiest moments of his life — especially his earliest childhood, when he used to be undressed and put to bed, when his nurse would lean over him and sing him to sleep, and he, burying his head in the pillow, felt happy in the sheer awareness of being alive — came back to him, not merely as something past but as something present.
The doctors were busy with the wounded man whose head had seemed so familiar. They were lifting him up, trying to calm him.
"Show it to me... Oh, ooh... Oh! Oh, ooh!" his frightened moans could be heard, subdued by pain and broken by sobs.

Hearing those moans, Prince Andrew wanted to weep. Whether because he was dying without glory, or because he was sorry to leave life, or because of those memories of a childhood that could never return, or because he was suffering and others were suffering and that man beside him was moaning so pitifully — he felt like weeping childlike, gentle, almost happy tears.
The wounded man was shown his amputated leg, caked in dried blood with the boot still on.
"Oh! Oh, ooh!" he sobbed, like a woman.
The doctor who had been blocking Prince Andrew's view stepped aside.
"My God! What is this? Why is he here?" Prince Andrew said to himself.

In the wretched, sobbing, weakened man whose leg had just been amputated, he recognized Anatole Kuragin. Men were supporting him in their arms and offering him a glass of water, but his trembling, swollen lips couldn't grasp its rim. Anatole was sobbing painfully. "Yes, it is him! Yes, that man is somehow closely and painfully connected with me," thought Prince Andrew, not yet clearly grasping what he saw. "What is the connection between that man and my childhood and my life?" he asked himself, finding no answer. And suddenly a new, unexpected memory from that realm of pure and loving childhood came to him. He remembered Natasha as he had first seen her at the ball in 1810, with her slender neck and arms and her frightened, happy face ready for joy — and love and tenderness for her, stronger and more vivid than ever, awakened in his soul. He now remembered the connection between himself and this man who was gazing at him dimly through tears filling his swollen eyes. He remembered everything, and an ecstatic pity and love for that man overflowed his happy heart.
Prince Andrew could no longer hold back and wept tender, loving tears for his fellow men, for himself, and for all their mistakes.

"Compassion, love for our brothers, for those who love us and for those who hate us, love of our enemies — yes, that love which God preached on earth and which Princess Mary taught me and I did not understand — that is what made me sorry to leave life, that is what remained for me had I lived. But now it is too late. I know it!"
